headline: High: ctx can write shared files and observe Claude Code events while opik has broad network egress, creating default-path leakage and cascading-error risk.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ctx can observe Claude Code PostToolUse and Stop events and uses filesystem surfaces, so if opik outputs are bridged into shared files or prompts, instruction-like content could be re-ingested. opik has broad network egress but no direct parsing surface is documented, so the interaction is inferred and uncertain.
conditions: IF ctx reads opik-generated text from a shared file or hook output, then prompt injection is plausible.
IF opik content is manually copied into Claude Code prompts, then ctx may treat it as instructions.
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different workspaces.
Disable automatic ingestion of hook output into prompts.
Add a manual review step before ctx consumes opik text.
Use read-only exports for any opik artifacts shared with ctx.

B_data_leakage.rationale: ctx touches audit/runtime logs, graph data, and filesystem content, while opik has broad network egress and REST API access. Even without a shared workspace explicitly documented, any shared files or logs could move sensitive ctx data into opik-backed network paths. The pairwise leakage pathway is plausible but not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF ctx writes sensitive logs or graph data into a location opik reads, then leakage occurs.
IF opik transmits received context to its REST API, then shared-file data can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Keep ctx logs in a separate directory from opik inputs.
Redact sensitive fields before any handoff.
Block network egress for opik during shared-data processing.
Use per-agent service accounts and separate credentials.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ctx supports multiple instances and filesystem writes, while opik has REST API/network egress. If both operate on the same mutable workspace or shared resources, they can overwrite or race on artifacts. No locking or coordination primitive is documented, so uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, then file clobbering or race conditions can occur.
IF both agents mutate the same remote resource via API, then last-write-wins conflicts are possible.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories.
Serialize writes with a simple operator-managed lock file.
Make one agent read-only for shared artifacts.
Snapshot the workspace before concurrent runs.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ctx observes Claude Code events and can shape downstream context, while opik exposes REST API/network egress. If opik consumes ctx-produced summaries or logs as authoritative, errors can propagate into later actions or reports. There is no documented verification barrier, so the cascade is plausible in default workflows but not proven.
conditions: IF opik treats ctx output as ground truth without validation, then incorrect facts can cascade.
IF ctx emits malformed summaries that opik forwards to downstream systems, then the error propagates.
mitigations: Require a human check before opik forwards ctx-derived outputs.
Add schema validation on ctx outputs.
Log provenance for every ctx-to-opik handoff.
Reject outputs that lack source references.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only and no residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented. ctx touches audit/runtime logs and graph data, but opik lists no data classes or compliance constraints, so only a weak compliance concern exists. The other agent is not cited beyond its lack of documented controls.
conditions: IF ctx logs contain regulated data and opik stores or forwards them, then a policy mismatch may arise.
IF a deployment adds regulated data classes to opik, then retention/residency review is required.
mitigations: Confirm what data classes opik will receive.
Disable retention of shared logs by default.
Document a data-handling policy for ctx outputs.
Review residency requirements before enabling any shared pipeline.
